paras: The threats against Anderson Johnson followed his killing of his cousin Isaac Alfrey in Bath County, Kentucky, in early June 1881, and drove Johnson from his home under a warning of death. A widely reprinted wire brief said a mob had gone to hang him, but the Kentucky reports describe a court examination and an anonymous notice to leave rather than a mob. No report gives the race of either man.

Johnson and Alfrey were cousins and farmers living about half a mile apart, described by an Owingsville dispatch as members of "wealthy and prominent families." Their dispute concerned Alfrey's hogs, which kept getting into Johnson's corn field.

On a Sunday morning, which the Kentucky Gazette later dated June 6, Johnson shot and killed Alfrey in front of Licking Union church while Sunday school was in session. According to the Gazette, Alfrey had already fired one pistol shot at Johnson and was about to fire again, and Johnson turned the second barrel of his shotgun on Alfrey's armed son and made him put up his weapon.

Charged with murder, Johnson faced a preliminary examination at Owingsville before County Judge E. N. Brother beginning June 12, with a large defense team and a packed courtroom. A Dallas Herald dispatch of June 13 predicted that he would be held on bail, while the Gazette's badly printed later report appears to speak of his acquittal.

After the hearing Johnson stayed away from home, and when he returned on a Tuesday to see his family he received within about an hour an anonymous note ordering him to leave and not return "under penality of death." He left the same evening, crossed the river into Rowan County, and went to his father-in-law's house, where he remained.

His family later received notice to leave as well, and Johnson was reported to be planning to sell his farm and settle elsewhere. The Gazette's correspondent wrote that Alfrey's relatives believed the killing was a premeditated murder and expected them to take Johnson's life or that of one of his family, and that the neighborhood on both sides of the Licking was "greatly excited." No report of a mob reaching Johnson, of arrests for the threats, or of a later trial was found in the coverage.

The killing reached papers in two forms. Kentucky dispatches, carried by the Omaha Daily Bee, the Lexington Kentucky Gazette and the Dallas Daily Herald, treated it as a homicide between prominent cousins and followed the court hearing, and Ohio papers ran a short "Murder in Kentucky" item that misprinted the county as "Barth."

The New York Sun's "Sunbeams" column of June 13 retold it as a comic chain in which a dog bit a hog and each man shot the other's animal, ending with "the latest report" of a mob going "to hang the murderer." That brief was reprinted through mid-July in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Mississippi, Washington and Maryland, while a Missouri paper dropped the mob clause and an Ohio paper placed the town at "Owenville."

The mob rests on the wire brief alone; the local reports, written closer to the scene and later, describe an anonymous death threat and Johnson's flight instead. The brief also gives a dog bite as the start of the quarrel, where the Kentucky accounts give hogs trespassing in Johnson's corn.

bases: The only violence against Johnson that the local reports describe is an anonymous notice to leave on penalty of death and pressure from his victim's kin (A9, A10); the claim that a mob went to hang him comes from a single humorous wire brief (A3) with no follow-up.

No one was killed by a mob: Johnson was examined in court and later fled to Rowan County after a death threat (A4, A9, A10); the wire brief says only that a mob 'had gone to hang the murderer' and gives no outcome (A3).

The homicide is corroborated by independent reports (A1, A2, A4, A6), but the mob-hanging claim rests on one wire brief reprinted many times (A3), and the death-threat notice on one Kentucky Gazette report (A9, A10).

info: Johnson killed Alfrey on a Sunday morning in early June 1881; the Kentucky Gazette dates it 'Sunday June 6th' (June 6, 1881 fell on a Monday). The death-threat notice came on a later Tuesday, after the examining trial.
In front of Licking Union church, in the eastern/southern part of Bath County, on the Licking River near the Rowan County line; the examining trial was at Owingsville.
W. Anderson Johnson, the target of the threats; no race is stated for him or for Isaac Alfrey in any report.
Johnson was charged with the murder of his cousin Isaac Alfrey after a quarrel over Alfrey's hogs in his corn field; he claimed self-defense.
Wire brief: 'a mob'. Kentucky Gazette: an anonymous note-writer from the neighborhood; Alfrey's relatives and friends said to be determined to have Johnson's life or drive him away.
Johnson left home the evening he received the notice and stayed with his father-in-law in Rowan County; his family had been told to leave and was expected to; he intended to sell out and move.
